title: Indian Mom Harshana Loses 32 Kg in 11 Months, Quits Five Everyday Foods
excerpt: Gurugram-based work-from-home mother Deepti Harshana shared the everyday foods she quit — sugary drinks, white bread, packaged snacks, fried food and late-night snacking — alongside hydration, sleep and daily walking.
body:
• Gurugram-based content creator and work-from-home mother Deepti Harshana lost 32 kg in 11 months, sharing that she did it through sustained habit changes rather than a fad diet.
  • The five everyday foods she quit: sugary drinks, white bread, packaged snacks, fried fast food, and late-night snacking — swapping them for lemon water/coconut water/green tea, multigrain or sourdough bread and oats, roasted chana, nuts and makhana, homemade wraps and tikkas, and herbal tea before bed.
  • Beyond food, her routine included 2–3 litres of water daily, roughly seven hours of sleep, and regular walking — and she emphasized that a calorie deficit came first.
  • Weight loss varies by person: results that work for one body may not transfer, so diet and fitness changes should be tailored to individual needs and discussed with a qualified expert.

A work-from-home mother's 32-kg turnaround

When Deepti Harshana, a social media content creator based in Gurugram and a work-from-home mother, started documenting her weight-loss journey on Instagram, the results were striking: 32 kg gone in 11 months. There was no exotic superfood or expensive program behind it. In one widely shared Reel, she simply listed the everyday foods she had quit to reduce her weight and control bloating — and the plain substitutions that replaced them.

Her message was deliberately unglamorous. As she wrote in her caption, "You still need to be in a calorie deficit FIRST." The foods she gave up were habits, not ingredients from another cuisine — which is exactly why her story has resonated with so many ordinary Indian households.

What she quit, and what she swapped in

First off the list were sugary drinks. Instead of reaching for sweetened beverages, she switched to simpler options — lemon water, coconut water and green tea. In her account, sugary drinks contributed to fat storage and water retention, which showed up as a puffy face.

White bread went next, replaced by multigrain or whole-wheat bread, sourdough and oats. Packaged snacks — the salty, shelf-stable kind — were cut down because of their high salt content and the bloating she experienced; roasted chana, nuts and makhana became the snack drawer instead.

Fried fast food left her everyday menu in favor of homemade wraps, paneer or chicken tikka and simple home-cooked meals. And the fifth habit to go was late-night snacking: mindless eating after hours, she felt, added calories without any real hunger, so herbal tea before sleep took its place.

Beyond the plate

The food swaps were only part of the routine. Harshana also focused on hydration — 2 to 3 litres of water a day — slept roughly seven hours a night and walked regularly. The point she keeps returning to is consistency over intensity: simple, repeatable habits sustained across eleven months, not a short burst of deprivation.

It is worth noting that she frames the changes honestly — as things that worked for her body and helped her stay on track, not as a prescription. Weight loss is driven by overall calorie intake, activity, sleep and individual health, and the same swaps will not produce the same outcome for everyone.

What this means for readers in the diaspora

For Indian-American families, Harshana's story has an obvious familiarity: the snacks she quit — packaged namkeen, white bread, sugary chai-adjacent drinks — sit in diaspora pantries too. Her swaps are equally portable: makhana and roasted chana are already staples in many Indian-American kitchens, and the real lesson is process — cut the quiet daily calories first, keep the sleep and movement steady, and let the deficit do the work.

A measured takeaway

No single story is a medical recommendation. Harshana's journey is motivating precisely because it is ordinary — small substitutions, repeated daily, adding up over nearly a year. Readers considering changes of their own should consult a qualified professional to tailor the approach to their health, body and lifestyle.
